```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.2,
                      out.width = "100%")
has_survey <- requireNamespace("survey", quietly = TRUE)
has_mgcv <- requireNamespace("mgcv", quietly = TRUE)
```

```{r packages, message = FALSE}
library(ipw)
library(survival)
```

ipw estimates **inverse probability weights**: each person is weighted by the
inverse of the probability of the exposure they actually received, given
their confounders. In the weighted data, exposure no longer depends on the
measured confounders, and a simple model of outcome on exposure, a
**marginal structural model (MSM)**, estimates the causal effect (Robins,
Hernán & Brumback 2000; van der Wal & Geskus 2011).

An analysis has three steps:

1. **Estimate the weights** with `ipwpoint()` (exposure measured once) or
   `ipwtm()` (exposure that changes over time), or from your own
   probabilities with `ipwprob()`.
2. **Check the weights** with `summary()` and `ipwplot()`.
3. **Fit the MSM** with the weights, and get **standard errors**, preferably
   with `ipwboot()`.

| Function | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `ipwpoint()` | Weights for an exposure measured once (point treatment) |
| `ipwtm()` | Weights for an exposure that changes over time, and censoring weights |
| `ipwprob()` | Weights from probabilities you estimated yourself **(new)** |
| `ipwboot()` | Bootstrap standard errors that re-estimate the weights **(new)** |
| `ipwplot()` | Plot the distribution of the weights |
| `tstartfun()` | Interval start times for counting-process (Cox) data |

> **New in the development version.** Sections marked **New** describe
> features added after ipw 1.3.2: count, gamma and log-normal exposures,
> smooth terms with mgcv, ATT and overlap weights, `type = "all"` for
> categorical and survival exposures in `ipwtm()`, `ipwprob()` and
> `ipwboot()`. Existing calls give the same results as before.

# 1. Point treatment: a binary exposure

We simulate a confounder `l`, a binary exposure `a` that is more likely at
high `l`, and an outcome `y`. The true causal effect of `a` on `y` is 10.

```{r simdat}
set.seed(16)
n <- 1000
simdat <- data.frame(l = rnorm(n, 10, 5))
simdat$a <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(simdat$l - 10))
simdat$y <- 10 * simdat$a + 0.5 * simdat$l + rnorm(n, -10, 5)
```

`ipwpoint()` fits the exposure model (here a logistic regression) and returns
the weights. With `numerator = ~ 1` the weights are **stabilized**: the
marginal probability of the exposure goes in the numerator, which keeps the
correction but makes the weights much less variable.

```{r ipwpoint}
w <- ipwpoint(exposure = a, family = "binomial", link = "logit",
              numerator = ~ 1, denominator = ~ l, data = simdat)
summary(w$ipw.weights)
ipwplot(weights = w$ipw.weights, logscale = FALSE, main = "Stabilized weights",
        xlim = c(0, 8))
```

Stabilized weights should have a mean close to 1. The exposure models are
returned as well, so they can be checked like any regression:

```{r models}
coef(w$den.mod)
```

The weighted regression of `y` on `a` estimates the causal effect; the
unweighted regression is confounded by `l`:

```{r msm}
c(unweighted = unname(coef(lm(y ~ a, data = simdat))["a"]),
  weighted   = unname(coef(lm(y ~ a, data = simdat, weights = w$ipw.weights))["a"]))
```

For inference, the weighted model is usually fitted with robust standard
errors, for example with the survey package as in the JSS paper; see
section 7 for why the bootstrap is better.

```{r svyglm, eval = has_survey}
msm <- survey::svyglm(y ~ a, design = survey::svydesign(~ 1, weights = ~ w$ipw.weights,
                                                        data = simdat))
cbind(estimate = coef(msm), confint(msm))["a", ]
```

**Unstabilized weights** use `numerator = NULL` (the default), and
**truncation** caps extreme weights at chosen percentiles:

```{r trunc}
w.unstab <- ipwpoint(exposure = a, family = "binomial", link = "logit",
                     denominator = ~ l, data = simdat)
w.trunc <- ipwpoint(exposure = a, family = "binomial", link = "logit",
                    numerator = ~ 1, denominator = ~ l, data = simdat, trunc = 0.01)
rbind(unstabilized = summary(w.unstab$ipw.weights),
      stabilized   = summary(w$ipw.weights),
      truncated    = summary(w.trunc$weights.trunc))
```

## New: ATT and overlap weights

The weights above target the **average treatment effect (ATE)**: the effect
if everyone versus no one were exposed. With `estimand = "ATT"` the weights
target the effect **in the exposed** (exposed get weight 1, unexposed
p/(1 - p)); with `estimand = "ATO"`, **overlap weights**, the effect in the
people whose exposure was most uncertain (exposed 1 - p, unexposed p, all
between 0 and 1). Here p is the fitted probability of exposure.

```{r estimands}
fit.estimand <- function(estimand) {
  wt <- ipwpoint(exposure = a, family = "binomial", link = "logit",
                 denominator = ~ l, data = simdat, estimand = estimand)$ipw.weights
  c(effect = unname(coef(lm(y ~ a, data = simdat, weights = wt))["a"]),
    max.weight = max(wt))
}
sapply(c(ATE = "ATE", ATT = "ATT", ATO = "ATO"), fit.estimand)
```

The effect was simulated as constant, so all three estimands are 10 in
truth, and the differences between the estimates are sampling noise. The
ATT weights show why: unexposed people with a high probability of exposure
get weights above 100, which makes that estimate unstable. Overlap weights
never exceed 1, which helps when some people are almost always or almost
never exposed. With an effect that differs between people, the three
estimands differ in truth as well.

# 2. Point treatment: other kinds of exposure

## Categorical and ordered exposures

For an exposure with more than two categories, `family = "multinomial"` fits
a multinomial logistic model and `family = "ordinal"` a proportional-odds
model (with `link = "logit"`, `"probit"`, `"cauchit"` or `"cloglog"`).

```{r categorical}
set.seed(4)
cat.dat <- data.frame(l = rnorm(800))
eta <- 0.9 * cat.dat$l
cat.dat$dose <- cut(eta + rlogis(800), c(-Inf, -0.5, 0.8, Inf),
                    labels = c("low", "medium", "high"), ordered_result = TRUE)
w.ord <- ipwpoint(exposure = dose, family = "ordinal", link = "logit",
                  numerator = ~ 1, denominator = ~ l, data = cat.dat)
w.mult <- ipwpoint(exposure = dose, family = "multinomial",
                   numerator = ~ 1, denominator = ~ l, data = cat.dat)
rbind(ordinal = summary(w.ord$ipw.weights), multinomial = summary(w.mult$ipw.weights))
```

## Continuous exposures

`healthdat` contains IQ, monthly income and a health score for 1000
simulated people; IQ confounds the effect of income on health. For a
continuous exposure the weights use densities instead of probabilities, so a
numerator model is required.

```{r gaussian}
data(healthdat)
w.gauss <- ipwpoint(exposure = income, family = "gaussian",
                    numerator = ~ 1, denominator = ~ iq, data = healthdat)
summary(w.gauss$ipw.weights)
coef(lm(health ~ income, data = healthdat, weights = w.gauss$ipw.weights))
```

### New: skewed continuous exposures (gamma and log-normal)

Many exposures are positive with a long right tail, such as a dose or a
duration: most values are small and a few are very large. A normal model is
symmetric and fits that tail poorly, and the tail is where weights become
large. `family = "gamma"` (log link) and `family = "lognormal"` (a normal
model for the log of the exposure) are meant for such exposures; both
require positive values. Below, the exposure is log-normal given `l`, and
the true effect of one unit of `dose` on `y` is 1.

```{r skewed}
set.seed(8)
sk <- data.frame(l = rnorm(1000))
sk$dose <- exp(0.5 + 0.5 * sk$l + rnorm(1000, 0, 0.6))
sk$y <- sk$dose + 2 * sk$l + rnorm(1000)
c(mean = mean(sk$dose), median = median(sk$dose))   # right-skewed

fit.dose <- function(family) {
  wt <- ipwpoint(exposure = dose, family = family, numerator = ~ 1,
                 denominator = ~ l, data = sk)$ipw.weights
  c(effect = unname(coef(lm(y ~ dose, data = sk, weights = wt))["dose"]),
    mean.weight = mean(wt), max.weight = max(wt))
}
sapply(c(gaussian = "gaussian", gamma = "gamma", lognormal = "lognormal"), fit.dose)
```

Choose the family by looking at the exposure: if it is right-skewed and
looks bell-shaped after taking logs, use `"lognormal"`; if its spread grows
with its mean, `"gamma"`. Do not use them for an exposure that is roughly
symmetric: income in `healthdat` (mean and median both about 2700) is
modelled well by `"gaussian"`, and a log-normal model there gives a few
people with very low income enormous weights.

### New: count exposures (Poisson and negative binomial)

For counts, such as a number of visits, `family = "poisson"` fits a Poisson
model and `family = "negbin"` a negative binomial model (via
`MASS::glm.nb`) that allows more spread than the Poisson. Here the true
effect of each extra visit on `y` is 0.5.

```{r counts}
set.seed(6)
cnt <- data.frame(l = rnorm(1000))
cnt$visits <- rnbinom(1000, size = 2, mu = exp(0.5 + 0.4 * cnt$l))
cnt$y <- 0.5 * cnt$visits + cnt$l + rnorm(1000)
c(mean = mean(cnt$visits), variance = var(cnt$visits))   # variance > mean
w.pois <- ipwpoint(exposure = visits, family = "poisson",
                   numerator = ~ 1, denominator = ~ l, data = cnt)
w.nb <- ipwpoint(exposure = visits, family = "negbin",
                 numerator = ~ 1, denominator = ~ l, data = cnt)
sapply(list(poisson = w.pois, negbin = w.nb), function(x)
  c(effect = unname(coef(lm(y ~ visits, data = cnt, weights = x$ipw.weights))["visits"]),
    max.weight = max(x$ipw.weights)))
```

The variance is clearly larger than the mean, so the negative binomial model
is the better choice for these data.

## New: smooth terms with mgcv

A regression assumes a straight-line effect of each confounder on the logit
of the exposure probability. When the true relation is curved, the weights
leave residual confounding. Writing `s(l)` in a formula fits the exposure
model as a generalized additive model with mgcv, which estimates the shape
of the curve from the data. Smooth terms work in `ipwpoint()` for the
binomial, gaussian and Poisson families and in `ipwtm()` for the binomial
family. The true effect below is 2.

```{r gam, eval = has_mgcv}
set.seed(10)
nl <- data.frame(l = runif(2000, -2, 2))
nl$a <- rbinom(2000, 1, plogis(2 * sin(1.5 * nl$l)))
nl$y <- 2 * nl$a + 3 * sin(1.5 * nl$l) + rnorm(2000)

w.lin <- ipwpoint(exposure = a, family = "binomial", link = "logit",
                  numerator = ~ 1, denominator = ~ l, data = nl)
w.gam <- ipwpoint(exposure = a, family = "binomial", link = "logit",
                  numerator = ~ 1, denominator = ~ s(l), data = nl)
c(unweighted   = unname(coef(lm(y ~ a, data = nl))["a"]),
  linear.model = unname(coef(lm(y ~ a, data = nl, weights = w.lin$ipw.weights))["a"]),
  smooth.model = unname(coef(lm(y ~ a, data = nl, weights = w.gam$ipw.weights))["a"]))
```

`plot(w.gam$den.mod)` shows the fitted curve. A covariate that is simply
named `s`, `te`, `ti` or `t2` is treated as an ordinary variable.

# 3. Exposure that changes over time

## HAART and mortality (`haartdat`)

`haartdat` contains simulated follow-up of 1200 HIV-infected patients from
seroconversion, one row per 100 days. Patients can start HAART (`haartind`
becomes 1 and stays 1). CD4 count is a time-varying confounder: low CD4
leads to starting HAART and to death, and HAART raises CD4. Ordinary
adjustment for CD4 would remove part of the effect of HAART; weighting does
not.

```{r haartdat}
data(haartdat)
head(haartdat[, c("patient", "tstart", "fuptime", "haartind", "event", "cd4.sqrt", "dropout")])
```

`ipwtm()` with `family = "survival"` fits Cox models for the time to
starting HAART. With `type = "first"`, each patient contributes until HAART
is started, because afterwards starting is no longer a choice. A second set
of weights corrects for **informative censoring**: dropout also depends on
CD4.

```{r ipwtm}
w.haart <- ipwtm(exposure = haartind, family = "survival",
                 numerator = ~ sex + age, denominator = ~ sex + age + cd4.sqrt,
                 id = patient, tstart = tstart, timevar = fuptime,
                 type = "first", data = haartdat)
w.cens <- ipwtm(exposure = dropout, family = "survival",
                numerator = ~ sex + age, denominator = ~ sex + age + cd4.sqrt,
                id = patient, tstart = tstart, timevar = fuptime,
                type = "cens", data = haartdat)
summary(w.haart$ipw.weights * w.cens$ipw.weights)
ipwplot(weights = w.haart$ipw.weights, timevar = haartdat$fuptime, binwidth = 100,
        main = "Stabilized weights for starting HAART")
```

The MSM is a weighted Cox model for death with the product of the two
weights:

```{r haart-msm}
msm.haart <- coxph(Surv(tstart, fuptime, event) ~ haartind + cluster(patient),
                   data = haartdat, weights = w.haart$ipw.weights * w.cens$ipw.weights)
summary(msm.haart)$conf.int
```

`tstartfun()` builds the interval start times needed for such data from
the end times:

```{r tstartfun}
toy <- data.frame(patient = c(1, 1, 1, 2, 2), time = c(14, 34, 41, 0, 11))
toy$tstart <- tstartfun(patient, time, toy)
toy
```

Other families work in `ipwtm()` as well: `"binomial"` (pooled logistic
regression), `"multinomial"`, `"ordinal"` and `"gaussian"` (GEE, with
`type = "all"`).

## New: categorical exposures that switch back and forth

With `type = "all"`, every interval contributes the probability of the
category observed in it, so an exposure can move between categories in
both directions. This now works for multinomial and ordinal exposures. The
models are pooled over time, so **past exposure belongs in the formulas**;
here the previous dose level `dose.lag`.

```{r type-all-ordinal}
set.seed(3)
n.id <- 300
long <- data.frame(id = rep(seq_len(n.id), each = 4), time = rep(1:4, times = n.id))
long$l <- rnorm(nrow(long))
long$dose <- NA
long$dose.lag <- NA
for (t in 1:4) {
  rows <- long$time == t
  prev <- if (t == 1) rep(1, n.id) else long$dose[long$time == t - 1]
  eta <- -1 + 0.8 * long$l[rows] + 0.7 * (prev - 1)
  u <- runif(n.id)
  long$dose.lag[rows] <- prev
  long$dose[rows] <- ifelse(u < plogis(eta - 1.5), 3, ifelse(u < plogis(eta), 2, 1))
}
long$dose <- factor(long$dose, levels = 1:3, labels = c("low", "medium", "high"),
                    ordered = TRUE)

w.dose <- ipwtm(exposure = dose, family = "ordinal", link = "logit",
                numerator = ~ dose.lag, denominator = ~ dose.lag + l,
                id = id, timevar = time, type = "all", data = long)
summary(w.dose$ipw.weights)
ipwplot(weights = w.dose$ipw.weights, timevar = long$time, binwidth = 1,
        main = "Cumulative stabilized weights by visit")
```

## New: recurrent exposure events in survival models

`family = "survival"` previously allowed only `type = "first"`. With
`type = "all"` (Graffeo, Latouche, Geskus & Chevret 2018), the exposure
indicator marks an exposure event at the end of an interval, such as a new
prescription, that may happen **more than once** per person. An
Andersen-Gill Cox model is fitted on all rows, and each row contributes the
probability of the observed status over its own interval. The intervals may
be irregular and differ between people.

```{r survival-all}
set.seed(21)
n.id <- 300
rec <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(n.id), function(i) {
  k <- sample(3:6, 1)
  cuts <- sort(runif(k))
  data.frame(id = i, tstart = c(0, cuts[-k]), fuptime = cuts)
}))
rec$x <- rep(rbinom(n.id, 1, 0.5), times = as.vector(table(rec$id)))  # fixed covariate
rec$xt <- rbinom(nrow(rec), 1, 0.4)                                    # time-varying
rec$expo <- rbinom(nrow(rec), 1, plogis(-1 + 0.5 * rec$x - rec$xt))   # exposure events

w.first <- ipwtm(exposure = expo, family = "survival", numerator = ~ x,
                 denominator = ~ x + xt, id = id, tstart = tstart, timevar = fuptime,
                 type = "first", data = rec)
w.all <- ipwtm(exposure = expo, family = "survival", numerator = ~ x,
               denominator = ~ x + xt, id = id, tstart = tstart, timevar = fuptime,
               type = "all", data = rec)
c(rows.used.first = sum(w.first$selvar), rows.used.all = sum(w.all$selvar))
rbind(first = summary(w.first$ipw.weights), all = summary(w.all$ipw.weights))
```

With `type = "first"`, the rows after a person's first exposure event are
ignored; with `type = "all"` they all count. For a treatment that is
started and stopped, Graffeo et al. compute weights separately for starting
(on the rows off treatment) and for stopping (on the rows on treatment).

# 4. New: weights from your own probabilities

`ipwprob()` turns probabilities you estimated yourself, for example with a
machine-learning model or SuperLearner, into weights. Give the probability
(or density) of the exposure each person actually received; with `id` and
`timevar`, the ratios are multiplied over time within each person. Below, a
cubic logistic model stands in for a flexible learner.

```{r ipwprob}
p.flex <- fitted(glm(a ~ poly(l, 3), family = binomial, data = simdat))
w.own <- ipwprob(den = ifelse(simdat$a == 1, p.flex, 1 - p.flex),
                 num = ifelse(simdat$a == 1, mean(simdat$a), 1 - mean(simdat$a)))
summary(w.own$ipw.weights)
coef(lm(y ~ a, data = simdat, weights = w.own$ipw.weights))["a"]

# time-varying: ratios multiplied within each person, in time order
toy <- data.frame(id = c(1, 1, 2, 2), time = c(1, 2, 1, 2), p = c(0.5, 0.8, 0.4, 0.9))
ipwprob(den = toy$p, id = toy$id, timevar = toy$time)$ipw.weights
```

The warning from `glm()` is a reminder of the main risk: flexible models can
produce probabilities close to 0 or 1 and therefore extreme weights. Check
the weights and consider `trunc`.

# 5. New: bootstrap standard errors with `ipwboot()`

Robust (sandwich) standard errors treat the weights as known. In
simulations of weighted Cox models, Austin (2016) found naive standard
errors too small and robust standard errors too large; only the bootstrap
that **re-estimates the weights in each bootstrap sample** gave correct
standard errors and confidence intervals.

`ipwboot()` does the resampling. You write a function that takes a data set
and returns the estimate, computing the weights itself:

```{r boot-point}
msm.effect <- function(d) {
  wt <- ipwpoint(exposure = a, family = "binomial", link = "logit",
                 numerator = ~ 1, denominator = ~ l, data = d)$ipw.weights
  coef(lm(y ~ a, data = d, weights = wt))["a"]
}
set.seed(1)
boot.point <- ipwboot(simdat, msm.effect, R = 200)
boot.point
confint(boot.point, level = 0.90)
```

For data with several rows per person, give `id`: whole people are
resampled with all their rows, and each sampled copy gets a new identifier,
so someone drawn twice counts as two people. Here both sets of weights for
the HAART example are re-estimated in each sample (use about 200 samples in
practice; 20 keep this vignette quick):

```{r boot-haart}
haart.effect <- function(d) {
  w1 <- ipwtm(exposure = haartind, family = "survival", numerator = ~ sex + age,
              denominator = ~ sex + age + cd4.sqrt, id = patient,
              tstart = tstart, timevar = fuptime, type = "first", data = d)
  w2 <- ipwtm(exposure = dropout, family = "survival", numerator = ~ sex + age,
              denominator = ~ sex + age + cd4.sqrt, id = patient,
              tstart = tstart, timevar = fuptime, type = "cens", data = d)
  coef(coxph(Surv(tstart, fuptime, event) ~ haartind, data = d,
             weights = w1$ipw.weights * w2$ipw.weights))
}
set.seed(2)
boot.haart <- ipwboot(haartdat, haart.effect, id = patient, R = 20)
boot.haart
c(robust.se = unname(sqrt(diag(vcov(msm.haart)))), bootstrap.se = unname(boot.haart$se))
```

`ipwboot()` also supports `strata` (resampling within groups) and records
samples in which the analysis fails instead of stopping. Set a seed with
`set.seed()` for reproducible results.

# 6. Checking the weights

* **Mean close to 1.** Stabilized weights should average about 1; a mean far
  from 1 suggests a misspecified exposure model.
* **Extreme weights.** Very large weights point to **positivity** problems:
  some kinds of people (almost) never receive one of the exposures. Look at
  `ipwplot()`, reconsider the model, use overlap weights (`estimand = "ATO"`)
  or truncate (`trunc`), keeping in mind that truncation slightly changes
  what is estimated.
* **Assumptions.** The weighted analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding,
  positivity, consistency and correctly specified exposure (and censoring)
  models.

# References

* Austin PC (2016). Variance estimation when using inverse probability of
  treatment weighting (IPTW) with survival analysis. *Statistics in
  Medicine* 35, 5642-5655. doi:10.1002/sim.7084.
* Cole SR, Hernán MA (2008). Constructing inverse probability weights for
  marginal structural models. *American Journal of Epidemiology* 168,
  656-664.
* Graffeo N, Latouche A, Geskus RB, Chevret S (2018). Modeling time-varying
  exposure using inverse probability of treatment weights. *Biometrical
  Journal* 60, 323-332. doi:10.1002/bimj.201600223.
* Li F, Morgan KL, Zaslavsky AM (2018). Balancing covariates via propensity
  score weighting. *Journal of the American Statistical Association* 113,
  390-400.
* Robins JM, Hernán MA, Brumback B (2000). Marginal structural models and
  causal inference in epidemiology. *Epidemiology* 11, 550-560.
* van der Wal WM, Geskus RB (2011). ipw: An R package for inverse
  probability weighting. *Journal of Statistical Software* 43(13), 1-23.
  doi:10.18637/jss.v043.i13.
